'''vacationist''' (vā-kā′shọn-ist), ''n.'' [< ''vacation'' + ''-ist.''] One who is taking a vacation; especially, one who is journeying for pleasure; an excursionist. [Colloq.]

'''vacationless''' (vā-kā′shọn-les), ''a.'' [< ''vacation'' + ''-less.''] Without a vacation; deprived of a vacation.

'''vacatur''' (vā-kā′tėr), ''n.'' [< ML. ''vacatur'', 3d pers. pres. ind. pass. of ''vacare'', make void, trans. use of L. ''vacare'', be empty or void: see ''vacate.''] In ''law'', the act of annulling or setting aside.

'''vaccary''' (vak′a̤-ri), ''n.''; pl. ''vaccaries'' (-riz). [< ML. ''vaccaria'', < L. ''vacca'', a cow: see ''vaccine.'' Cf. ''vachery'', a doublet of ''vaccary.''] A cow-house, dairy, or cow-pasture. See ''vachery.'' [Prov. Eng.]
{{smaller block|At this time there were eleven ''vaccaries'' (places of pasture for cows) in Pendle Forest, and the herbage and agistments of each ''vaccary'' were valued to the lord at 10''s.'', or in all 110''s.'' yearly.
{{right|''Baines'', Hist. Lancashire, II. 25.}}}}

'''vaccigenous''' (vak-sij′e-nus), ''a.'' [Irreg. < ''vaccine'' + L. ''-gerere'', carry.] Producing vaccine: applied to methods of cultivating vaccine virus, or to farms and institutions where the virus is produced in quantity.

'''vaccin''' (vak′sin), ''n.'' Same as ''vaccine.''

'''vaccina''' (vak-sī′nä̤), ''n.'' [NL., < L. ''vaccinus'', of or from cows: see ''vaccine.''] Same as ''vaccinia.'' ''Dunglison.''

'''vaccinal''' (vak′si-nal), ''a.'' [< ''vaccine'' + ''-al.''] Of or relating to vaccine; caused by vaccination. ''Med. News'', LII. 546.—'''Vaccinal erythema,'''

As initial, it is almost solely of Romanic (French-Latin) origin, altered in pronunciation from the semi-vowel or ''w''-sound, which belonged to the same sign in Roman use (see ''W''). At the end of a word (where, however, it is never written without a following ''e''), it is found in many words of Germanic origin, often alternating with its surd counterpart ''f'', as in ''wife'', ''wives'', ''half'', ''halve'', etc.}}
'''2.''' As a Roman numeral, V stands for 5; with a dash over it (V̄), 5,000.—'''3.''' [''l. c.''] An abbreviation of ''velocity'' (in physics); ''verb; verse; versus'' (in law); ''vert'' (in heraldry); ''vision'' (in medicine); of ''verte'', ''violino'', ''voce'', and ''volta'' (in music); of ''ventral'' (fin), etc.—'''4.''' The chemical symbol of ''vanadium.''

'''V<sup>2</sup>''' (vē), ''n.'' [From the letter ''V.''] A five-dollar bill: so called from the character V which is conspicuous upon it. [Colloq., U. S.]

'''va''' (vä). [< It. ''va'' (= F. ''va''), go, go on, also ''vada'' (< L. ''vadere'', go), used as impv. 2d pers. sing. of ''andare'' = F. ''aller'', go: see ''wade''.] In ''music'', go on; continue: as, ''va crescendo'', go on increasing the strength of tone; ''va rallentando'', continue dragging the time.

'''vaagmar''' (väg′mär), ''n.'' [< Icel. ''vāg-meri'', a kind of flounder, ‘wave-mare,’ < ''vāg'', wave (see ''waw''<sup>1</sup>), + ''meri'', mare: see ''mare''<sup>1</sup>.] The deal-fish.

'''vaalite''' (vä′līt), ''n.'' [< ''Vaal'', a river in South Africa, + ''-ite''<sup>2</sup>.] A kind of vermiculite occasionally found associated with the diamond at the diggings in South Africa. It is probably an altered form of a mica (biotite) belonging to the original peridotite.

'''vacance†''' (vā′kans), ''n.'' [< F. ''vacance'' = Sp. Pg. ''vacancia'' = It. ''vacanzia'', ''vacanza'', < ML. ''vacantia'', empty place, vacancy, vacation, < L. ''vacan(t-)s'', empty, vacant: see ''vacant.''] Vacation. [Obsolete Scotch.]
{{smaller block|The consistory had no ''vacance'' at this Yool, but had little to do.
{{right|''Spalding'', Hist. Troubles in Scotland, i. 331. (''Jamieson.'')}}}}

'''vacancy''' (vā′kan-si), ''n.''; pl. ''vacancies'' (-siz). [As ''vacance'' (see ''-cy'').] '''1.''' The state of being vacant, empty, or unoccupied.
{{smaller block|The inquisitive, in my opinion, are such merely from a ''vacancy'' in their own imaginations.
{{right|''Steele'', Spectator, No. 282.}}}}
'''2.''' Specifically, emptiness of mind; idleness; listlessness.
{{smaller block|All dispositions to idleness or ''vacancy'', even before they grow habits, are dangerous.
{{right|''Sir H. Wotton'', Reliquiæ, p. 85.}}
At chesse they will play all the day long, a sport that agreeth well with their sedentary ''vacancy.''
{{right|''Sandys'', Travailes, p. 50.}}}}
'''3.''' That which is vacant or unoccupied. {{smaller|Specifically—(''a'') Empty space.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Alas, how is ’t with you,
That you do bend your eye on ''vacancy?''</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Hamlet, iii. 4. 117.}}}}
{{smaller|(''b'') An intermediate space; a gap; a chasm. A man could not perceive any ''vacant'' or wast place under the Alpes, but all beset with vines.
{{right|''Coryat'', Crudities, I. 81.}}}}
'''2.''' Not occupied or filled with an incumbent or tenant; unoccupied.
{{smaller block|<poem>Special dignities, which ''vacant'' lie
For thy best use and wearing.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', T. of A., v. 1. 145.}}
By . . . [Pelham’s] death, the highest post to which an English subject can aspire was left ''vacant''.
{{right|''Macaulay'', William Pitt.}}}}
'''3.''' Not engaged or filled with business or care; unemployed; unoccupied; free; disengaged; idle: as, ''vacant'' hours.
{{smaller block|Alexander, in tymes ''vacaunt'' from bataile, delyted in that maner huntinge. ''Sir T. Elyot'', The Governour, i. 18.
<poem>The loud laugh that spoke the ''vacant'' mind.</poem>
{{right|''Goldsmith'', Des. Vil., l. 122.}}
<poem>Absence of occupation is not rest;
A mind quite ''vacant'' is a mind distress’d.</poem>
{{right|''Cowper'', Retirement, l. 624.}}}}
'''4.''' Characterized by or proceeding from idleness or absence of mental occupation.
{{smaller block|Every morning waked us to a repetition of toil; but the evening repaid it with ''vacant'' hilarity. ''Goldsmith'', Vicar, v.}}
'''5.''' Free from thought; not given to thinking, study, reflection, or the like; thoughtless.
{{smaller block|You, who used to be so gay, so open, so ''vacant''!
{{right|''Steele'', Conscious Lovers, ii. 1.}}}}
'''6.''' Lacking, or appearing to lack, intelligence; stupid; inane.
{{smaller block|Rip stared in ''vacant'' stupidity.
{{right|''Irving'', Sketch-Book, p. 59.}}}} '''7.''' In ''law:'' (''a'') Not filled; unoccupied: as, a ''vacant'' office. (''b'') Empty: as, a ''vacant'' house. In the law of fire-insurance a house may be unoccupied, and yet not be deemed vacant. (''c'') Abandoned; having no heir: as, ''vacant'' effects or goods.—'''Vacant cylinder, lot, possession.''' {{smaller|See the nouns.}} ='''Syn. 1-4.''' {{smaller|''Vacant, Empty, Void, Devoid. Void'' and ''devoid'' are now used in a physical sense only in poetic or elevated diction; ''void'' is often used of laws, legal instruments, and the like: as, the will or deed or law was pronounced null and ''void. Devoid'' is now always followed by ''of:'' as, ''devoid of'' reason; a mind ''devoid of'' ideas. ''Vacant'' and ''empty'' are primarily physical: as, an ''empty'' box; a ''vacant'' lot. ''Empty'' is much the more general: it applies to that which contains nothing, whether previously filled or not: as, an ''empty'' bottle, drawer, nest, head. ''Vacant'' applies to that which has been filled or occupied, or is intended or is ready or needs to be filled or occupied: as, a ''vacant'' throne, chair, space, office, mind: an ''empty'' room has no furniture in it; a ''vacant'' room is one that is free for occupation. ''Vacant'' is a word of some dignity, and is therefore not used of the plainest things: we do not speak of a ''vacant'' box or bottle.}}

'''vacantly''' (vā′kạnt-li), ''adv.'' In a vacant manner; idly.

'''vacate''' (vā′kāt), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''vacated'', ppr. ''vacating.'' [< L. ''vacatus'', pp. of ''vacare'', be empty or vacant. From the same L. verb are ult. E. ''vacant'', ''vacuous'', ''vacuum'', etc. Cf. ''vain.''] '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To make vacant; cause to be empty;

{{c|6681 no validity: as, the ''vacation'' of a charter.}} '''2.''' A space of time, or a condition, in which there is an intermission of a stated employment or procedure; a stated interval in a round of duties; a holiday.
{{smaller block|<poem>To raise Recruits, and draw new Forces down,
Thus, in the dead ''Vacation'' of the Town.</poem>
{{right|''Congreve'', Pyrrhus, Prol.}}}}
{{smaller|Specifically—(''a'') In ''law'', temporary cessation of judicial proceedings; the space of time between the end of one term of court and the beginning of the next; the period during which a court holds no sessions; recess; non-term. In England the vacations are—Christmas vacation, commencing on December 24th and ending January 6th; Easter vacation, commencing on Good Friday and ending on Easter Tuesday; Whitsun vacation, commencing on the Saturday before and ending on the Tuesday after Whitsunday; and the long vacation, commencing on August 13th and ending on October 23d.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Why should not conscience have ''vacation''
As well as other courts o’ th’ nation?</poem>
{{right|''S. Butler'', Hudibras, II. ii. 317.}}}}
{{smaller|(''b'') The intermission of the regular studies of an educational institution of any kind, when the students have a recess; holidays: as, the summer ''vacation''.}}
'''3.''' The act of becoming vacant; avoidance: said especially of a see or other spiritual dignity.—'''4†.''' Freedom from duty; leisure time.
{{smaller block|<poem>Whan he hadde leyser and ''vacacioun''
From oother worldly occupacioun.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Prol. to Wife of Bath’s Tale, l. 683.}}}}
